bullets: Game 2 of 7 in a single-deck video; a win over a Miner / Evolution Inferno Dragon control deck (Goblin Cage, Goblin Brawler, Mega Minion, Ice Golem, Zap, Fireball), video time 174.3-370.0s. 'Good game. Nice win. I'll see you all in the next match' (t=362), with both enemy princess towers ground to 565 and 586 HP against his own 2927 and 3746 — no tower fell on either side. The in-game clock OCR failed for the whole video, so all timings are video seconds.

He states the deck's weakness and its edge in the first ten seconds: 'we don't have a lot of air defense, but he also doesn't have much bait defense. So it's going to be kind of difficult for both of us on the defensive end' (t=178-185). The air hole is real — the Evolution Inferno Dragon forces four-card defensive stacks at t=245-252 and t=294-303.

Core offensive loop: Goblin Barrel plus Fire Spirit in one lane, Wall Breakers in the other, repeated roughly every 25 seconds (t=212, 247, 261, 279, 304, 325, 338, 343, 355, 363), with the lane split chosen against the opponent's spell — 'It's going to be a lot of damage on the left side cuz I think he's going to Zap on the right' (t=264-267).

Success is measured in elixir drained, not damage: 'Just force out more elixir every single time' (t=283), 'force out another Goblin Cage. I think he's one card away though' (t=344-347), 'He spent all that elixir and we got damage' (t=349-350).

Wall Breakers double as the deck's kiting tool on defence (t=205.7 tile [10, 11], t=279.3 tile [3, 14]) so the real answers stay in hand, and he will skip the kite when it invites a spell — 'I do not think I need a Wall Breaker kite this Mega Minion though. Otherwise, he's going to just get a good Fireball here' (t=302-307).

The Ronin is played strictly as a defensive mini-tank on his own half (t=183.2 tile [8, 0], t=251.3 tile [2, 5]), never at the bridge, and he tempers the video's title in commentary: 'after the Ronin nerf it's not really a crazy card on top ladder, but it's a really good card for people who are either under-levelled or face a lot of Mega Knights and maybe a lot of mid-ladder decks... nothing insane, honestly' (t=225-243).

Bomb Tower is pre-placed centrally before pushes arrive (six placements) and Royal Delivery is the emergency air button (t=245.2, 297.3, 306.3); Magic Archer is played deep and early rather than at the bridge, and the one bridge Magic Archer is spell-predicted: 'Ooh, good prediction. He actually finally got me with one of those' (t=334-337).

new_deck.rationale: Goblin Barrel is the win condition with Wall Breakers, Ice Spirit and Fire Spirit baiting the small spell that answers it, while Bomb Tower, Royal Delivery and a defensive Ronin hold the ground until the barrel comes back around.
new_deck.why_it_works_md: The list is standard log bait with the Ronin taking the ground-defence slot: Goblin Barrel is the only real damage card, and Wall Breakers, Ice Spirit and Fire Spirit exist to make the opponent spend a spell or a building answer every cycle. Ryley plays it as an attrition deck rather than a burst one — he alternates barrel and Wall Breakers between lanes so a single Zap can never cover both, and grades every push by what it drained rather than what it hit: "Just force out more elixir every single time" (t=283). Defence is deliberately layered and cheap — Bomb Tower pre-placed centrally, Ice Spirit for resets, Fire Spirit for swarms, Royal Delivery as the panic button, and the Ronin parked on his own half as a mini-tank whose parry punishes single-target melee ("Goblin Brawler is pretty bad against the Ronin", t=191). The obvious hole is air: he says so out loud ("we don't have a lot of air defense", t=180) and an Evolution Inferno Dragon forces him to spend four cards on one push twice in this game. Wall Breakers pulling double duty as a defensive kite is what keeps that affordable.
